word_order: SVO — subjects precede verbs and objects follow them, e.g. 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device' and 'Mutations can have a variety of different effects'.
register: Edited written informational prose (news/encyclopedia/technical descriptions): generally formal, factual sentences with occasional instructional or descriptive passages.
clause_boundary_signals: coordinating conjunctions joining independent clauses (and, but)
subordinating conjunctions introducing dependent clauses (although, while)
relative/complementizer pronouns introducing clauses modifying NPs (who, that)
sentence-initial adverbials/parentheticals that open new sentential propositions (Of course, In reality)
non_boundary_traps: prepositional phrases inside noun phrases that resemble clause starts (of Venezuelans, of the piece)
possessive noun constructions and titles that look like genitive clauses (Branson's, bank’s)
numeric/quantifier phrases and measure expressions that are phrase-internal (Eighteen percent, Around 60)
noun compounds and names that contain multiple words but do not mark clause breaks (Virgin Group, Northern Rock bank)
unstable_prefix_signals: initial subordinators or adverbials after which scope/attachment is unresolved (although, while)
prepositional/temporal introducers whose role (clausal vs. phrase) is undecided until later context (prior to, because of)
focus/quantifier particles and short determiners that leave interpretation open until the following phrase (Only, Around 60)
notes_for_prompt_writer: Sentence structure is canonical English SVO with frequent embedded relative clauses and multiword temporal/causal connectors. Many long noun phrases contain prepositional modifiers, possessives, numerals, or titles that can be mistaken for clause starts. Watch for sentential parentheticals (e.g. 'Of course') and relative/complementizer words ('who', 'that') which reliably introduce subordinate material. No phonetic hesitation tokens appear in the sample.
